subject: Engelska 7
title: Reading comprehension: complex texts
sourceSummary: Implicit arguments, correlation versus causation, ironic/nuanced tone, and accurately summarising a complex line of reasoning.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Not everyone welcomed the new bypass. Local traders warned that reduced footpath traffic would hurt small shops, while environmental groups pointed to a modest drop in town-centre air pollution since it opened. The council's official statement praised improved 'traffic flow' without mentioning either concern. Meanwhile, three shops on the old high street have closed since construction began."

What implicit argument does the text make, without stating it directly?
questions.opener: Read between the lines: what does it reveal that the council does NOT mention, compared with what has actually happened (shops closing)?
choices: The bypass has been an unqualified success.
Traffic flow has improved dramatically.
The council may be avoiding uncomfortable questions about the bypass's local costs.
Environmental groups oppose the bypass.
questions.explanation: By setting the council's silence on the shop closures against the fact that three shops have closed, the text indirectly suggests that the council is avoiding uncomfortable questions. The text never states this outright, but the arrangement of facts carries the argument.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"A recent study found that towns with more cafés per capita also have higher average incomes. Some commentators have concluded that opening cafés boosts local wealth. Researchers behind the study, however, note that wealthier towns simply attract more café businesses in the first place, and caution against drawing causal conclusions from the data."

What is the main flaw in the commentators' conclusion?
questions.opener: The researchers themselves warn against a specific logical fallacy — which one?
choices: They assumed causation from a correlation that may run in the opposite direction.
They ignored the sample size of the study.
They misunderstood what 'per capita' means.
They confused income with wealth.
questions.explanation: The commentators interpret an association (correlation) as a cause (causation), even though the researchers point out that the causal relationship might run the other way — wealthy towns attract cafés, not the other way around. It's not about sample size or the meaning of the terms.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Ice cream sales and drowning incidents both rise sharply in the summer months. A tabloid headline claimed that 'eating ice cream increases drowning risk'."

What is missing from the tabloid's reasoning?
questions.opener: What probably causes both trends at the same time, without either one causing the other?
choices: A larger sample of drownings.
Consideration of a third factor — hot weather — that likely explains both trends.
Data from winter months.
A definition of 'drowning'.
questions.explanation: This is the classic example of a confounding variable: hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming (and therefore drowning risk). Neither variable causes the other.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Oh wonderful, another 'mandatory optional' training session. I'm sure my afternoon was crying out to be filled with a two-hour webinar on a policy nobody asked for. Truly, my career has been waiting for this moment."

What is the writer's tone?
questions.opener: The words say one thing, but the context ("mandatory optional", "crying out") signals the opposite.
choices: Genuinely enthusiastic
Neutral and informative
Anxious and apologetic
Ironic and sarcastic
questions.explanation: The phrase "mandatory optional" is a self-contradiction, and exaggeratedly positive words ("wonderful", "truly... waiting for this moment") about something the writer clearly dislikes is classic irony/sarcasm — the underlying meaning is the opposite of what's said.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Universal basic income (UBI) has been trialled in several countries. Advocates argue it reduces poverty and gives people freedom to retrain or start businesses. Critics counter that it is prohibitively expensive at scale and may reduce the incentive to work. Early trial results are mixed: poverty indicators improve, but long-term employment effects remain unclear due to short trial periods."

Which summary most accurately reflects the text?
questions.opener: A good summary weighs BOTH sides and the uncertainties the text actually mentions.
choices: UBI trials prove that basic income has no drawbacks.
UBI reduces poverty short-term, but its cost and long-term employment effects remain disputed.
UBI is too expensive and should be abandoned.
Critics have been proven wrong by trial data.
questions.explanation: The text presents a benefit (reduced poverty) and unresolved questions (cost, employment effects) without taking a side. Option 2 captures this balance; the others exaggerate or distort the text.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The company's annual report devotes four pages to its new recycling initiative and a single sentence to a 12% drop in full-time staff. Both changes occurred in the same fiscal year."

What can the reader reasonably infer about the report's purpose?
questions.opener: Compare how much space each piece of news gets — what does that say about what the company wants you to notice?
choices: The report proves the company only cares about the environment.
The staff reduction was unrelated to the recycling programme.
The report is purely factual with no persuasive intent.
The company wants to highlight the recycling initiative while downplaying the staff reduction.
questions.explanation: The uneven allocation of space (four pages versus one sentence) is a way of steering the reader's attention away from an uncomfortable piece of news — a common rhetorical device in annual reports. Option 1 claims too much; the text doesn't show that the company "only" cares about the environment.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and explain the logical flaw in the claim.

A news article states: 'Countries with more registered doctors per capita also report higher rates of certain diagnosed illnesses. This proves that doctors are causing disease.'
questions.opener: Consider whether there is a more reasonable explanation for the connection, without either variable causing the other.
questions.answer: The claim confuses correlation with causation: more doctors likely means better access to diagnosis, not that doctors cause illness.
steps: The text observes a correlation: more doctors per capita is associated with more diagnosed illnesses.
The conclusion "doctors are causing disease" is a causal claim that does not automatically follow from a correlation.
A more reasonable explanation: more doctors means better access to healthcare, which leads to MORE illnesses being detected and diagnosed — not more illnesses occurring.
This is an example of a confounding variable (access to healthcare) that explains both observations better than a direct causal relationship.

questions.prompt: Summarise key strategies for analysing complex texts: implicit argument, correlation vs causation, tone/irony, and accurate summary.
questions.opener: Four common pitfalls and how to avoid them on an advanced reading comprehension task.
questions.answer: Implicit argument: look for what the text does NOT say, and what is set against what (juxtaposition) · Correlation ≠ causation: ask whether a third factor could explain both trends (a confounding variable) · Irony/sarcasm: the words say one thing, the context/exaggeration reveals the opposite · Summary: weigh in ALL the sides the text presents, not just the one you agree with, and don't add conclusions the text doesn't support.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The press release celebrates a 'restructuring for future growth.' It does not mention that 200 employees lost their jobs in the process."

What does the omission suggest?
questions.opener: What does the press release's silence reveal, compared with what actually happened?
choices: The company is likely trying to present the layoffs in a more positive light by omitting them.
The layoffs were not significant enough to mention.
The press release is entirely objective and complete.
Future growth is guaranteed as a result of the restructuring.
questions.explanation: By celebrating a "restructuring for future growth" without mentioning that 200 people lost their jobs, the company is likely trying to cast the layoffs in a more positive light by omitting them.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Regions with more streetlights report lower crime rates. A city councillor proposed that installing more streetlights in all neighborhoods would directly reduce crime."

What should a careful reader question about this proposal?
questions.opener: Could a third factor explain both more streetlights and lower crime?
choices: Whether wealthier, safer areas simply already have more streetlights and lower crime for other reasons
Whether streetlights are too expensive to install
Whether the councillor understands what 'crime rate' means
Whether the study included enough cities
questions.explanation: A careful reader should question whether wealthier, already-safer areas simply already have more streetlights AND lower crime for other reasons, rather than the streetlights causing the lower crime.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Ah yes, because nothing says 'efficient meeting' like discussing the color of the new logo for forty-five minutes."

What tone does this sentence convey?
questions.opener: The words are exaggeratedly positive about something clearly inefficient — a sign of sarcasm.
choices: Sarcastic criticism of how the meeting's time was used
Genuine praise for the meeting's efficiency
A neutral description of the meeting's agenda
Confusion about what the meeting covered
questions.explanation: Calling a 45-minute discussion about a logo's color an "efficient meeting" is sarcastic criticism of how the meeting's time was used.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Proponents of a four-day school week cite improved teacher retention and student well-being. Opponents point to childcare difficulties for working parents and mixed academic results. Some districts report gains in math scores but declines in reading scores."

Which summary best reflects this text?
questions.opener: A good summary weighs in BOTH sides and the nuance in the results (math vs. reading).
choices: The four-day school week has both benefits and drawbacks, with academic effects that vary by subject.
The four-day school week is an unqualified success for all students.
The four-day school week should be abandoned immediately due to poor results.
Only teachers benefit from the four-day school week.
questions.explanation: The text presents both benefits (teacher retention, student well-being) and drawbacks (childcare, mixed academic results) without taking a side — option 1 captures this balance.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The advertisement shows only young, visibly fit people using the fitness app, despite the company's claim that it is 'designed for everyone.'"

What does this juxtaposition imply?
questions.opener: Compare what the advertisement SHOWS with what the company CLAIMS.
choices: There may be a gap between the company's stated inclusivity and how it actually markets the product.
The app is exclusively designed for elderly users.
The advertisement is factually inaccurate about the app's features.
Fitness apps are generally ineffective.
questions.explanation: Showing only young, fit people despite the claim "designed for everyone" suggests a gap between the company's stated inclusivity and how the product is actually marketed.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Students who eat breakfast tend to score higher on tests. A headline claims 'Eating breakfast makes you smarter.'"

What alternative explanation does the headline fail to consider?
questions.opener: Could a third factor (e.g. home circumstances) explain both breakfast habits and test scores?
choices: Students from stable, well-resourced households may be both more likely to eat breakfast and to perform well academically for unrelated reasons
Breakfast cereal companies funded the study
Test scores are not a valid measure of intelligence
Some students skip breakfast on test days only
questions.explanation: Students from stable, well-resourced households are likely both more likely to eat breakfast and to perform better in school for reasons unrelated to breakfast itself — a classic confounding variable the headline misses.

questions.prompt: "Of course, spending three hours in traffic on the way to a 'stress-free' vacation is exactly what everyone dreams of." Identify the rhetorical technique and its effect.
questions.opener: The word "stress-free" is set against the actual experience (three hours in traffic) — what does the contrast reveal?
choices: Irony — the writer highlights a contradiction between the label 'stress-free' and the actual experience
A literal, sincere description of an ideal vacation
A statistical claim about traffic patterns
An objective summary with no persuasive intent
questions.explanation: This is irony: the writer highlights the contradiction between the label "stress-free" and the actual, stressful experience in order to criticize the claim.
